prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Letter Violates the FDCPA Because the Least Sophisticated Debtor Could Reasonably Read It in More Than One Way, and One Reading Is Inaccurate.**

Congress enacted the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ("FDCPA") to eliminate abusive debt collection practices. Section 1692e prohibits a debt collector from using "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. That prohibition specifically reaches "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." *Id.* § 1692e(10). This Court construes the statute broadly to give effect to its remedial purpose. *See Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006).

**A. The least sophisticated debtor standard governs.**

Courts in this Circuit judge collection letters from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000); *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008). This objective standard protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 453–54. It also ensures that protection does not turn on any particular consumer's sophistication. *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298 (3d Cir. 2008). The standard is not unbounded. It presumes a debtor with "a quite low" level of sophistication who still reads the communication with some care and is capable of making basic inferences. *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221; *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The question is whether this hypothetical debtor could be misled. It is not whether the collector meant to mislead, and it is not whether a more sophisticated reader would see through the ambiguity. *See Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 148–49 (3d Cir. 2013); *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011).

**B. A letter is deceptive if it can reasonably be read to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.**

Under this Court's precedent, a collection letter is deceptive when it "can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221 (quoting *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455); *accord Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The collector does not escape liability by showing that the letter also supports an accurate reading. Once the inaccurate reading is a reasonable one for the least sophisticated debtor, the letter is actionable. *See Campuzano-Burgos*, 550 F.3d at 298–99; *Caprio*, 709 F.3d at 149–51. The rule follows from the standard itself. A least sophisticated debtor cannot be expected to resolve a collector's ambiguity in the collector's favor. The burden of clarity falls on the party that drafted the letter and controls its wording.

This Court has applied the rule consistently. In *Brown*, the Court held that the letter's statements about the debt could mislead the least sophisticated debtor, and it evaluated the letter as a whole. 464 F.3d at 454–55. In *Rosenau*, the Court asked whether the letter could reasonably be read to misrepresent the debtor's obligations, rather than whether it was defensible under the collector's own interpretation. 539 F.3d at 221–22. In *Lesher*, the Court looked at what the least sophisticated debtor would take from the letter's overall message, not what the collector claimed to intend. 650 F.3d at 997–99. And in *Douglass v. Convergent Outsourcing*, 765 F.3d 299, 303–04 (3d Cir. 2014), the Court again applied § 1692e's objective inquiry to the letter's actual effect on the least sophisticated debtor.

**C. Intent and actual deception are irrelevant, and the inaccuracy need only be material.**

Section 1692e is a strict-liability provision. A plaintiff need not show that the collector intended to deceive, or that the plaintiff was actually misled. *See Kaymark v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 783 F.3d 168, 174 (3d Cir. 2015); *Caprio*, 709 F.3d at 148–49. The inaccurate reading must be material, meaning it is capable of affecting the least sophisticated debtor's decision about how to respond to the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 419–21 (3d Cir. 2015). Materiality screens out only technical or immaterial misstatements. It does not excuse a letter that misleads the debtor about what is owed, to whom, or what the debtor may do next.

**D. Application.**

The letter here can reasonably be read two ways. Plaintiff's reading, which is inaccurate, is the one a least sophisticated debtor would likely adopt, and that reading would affect how the debtor responds. Under *Rosenau*, *Brown*, and *Wilson*, that ambiguity establishes a violation of § 1692e and § 1692e(10). Defendant's argument that a sophisticated reader could parse the letter accurately is therefore beside the point.
